title: Modeling smeared fiber-matrix pullout strength of steel fiber-reinforced concrete with various types of steel fiber and its tensile and compressive strength
abstract: This paper presents a novel smeared fiber-matrix pullout strength model for predicting the mechanical properties of steel fiber-reinforced concrete (SFRC). The model, developed within the fiber bridging stress framework, uniquely accounts for various fiber types (straight, hooked-end, and twisted) and their interaction with the cementitious matrix. The approach integrates critical factors including fiber orientation, embedment length, and matrix strength to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fiber bridging mechanism. Based on a database of 965 single-fiber pullout tests, formulas were we derived for predicting both tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC with single or hybrid steel fiber configurations. The model’s effectiveness is validated using separate databases containing 321 tensile and 1595 compressive strength test results across a wide range of concrete strengths (16.7–262 MPa). The model demonstrates adequate predictive capability, particularly for straight and hooked-end fibers, while showing some limitations for twisted fibers and fiber volume fractions above 3 %. This physically-significant approach not only provides a reliable tool for designing and optimizing SFRC materials but also offers new insights into the mechanisms of fiber reinforcement in concrete.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs:
Steel fiber-reinforced concrete (SFRC) has become one of the most widely used construction materials in structural engineering [1–5]  and bridge engineering [6–11]  over the past few decades due to its excellent mechanical properties, such as strength, toughness, energy absorption capacity, and durability. These properties are significantly enhanced by the inclusion of steel fibers and their fiber bridging effect. As shown in  
                      Fig. 1 , when micro-cracks develop within the concrete, tensile stress can be transferred from the matrix to the fibers due to the bond stress at the fiber-matrix interface. As a result, the steel fibers can continue to carry the tensile load at the micro-cracking plane, restraining the propagation of micro-cracks and thereby improving the tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC.

Tensile and compressive strengths are fundamental engineering properties of SFRC in practical applications. The impact of additional steel fibers on tensile strength has been comprehensively studied experimentally  [12–51] , as well as their effect on compressive strength  [38,39,48,52–286] . Some design-oriented models for predicting the tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC have been proposed, based on experimental results  [242,261,287–293] . Most of these models are phenomenologically derived from experimental data. Consequently, they express the enhancement effects on the strength of SFRC in various ways and often lack physical significance. For example, ACI 318–11  [288]  and JSCE-07  [289]  suggest that the splitting tensile strength of SFRC is independent of the properties and content of fibers. Additionally, the reinforcing index of SFRC,  R  =  V

However, most models do not consider the shape of the steel fiber (e.g., straight, hooked-end) or the influence of matrix strength on the bond strength at the fiber-matrix interface  [242,290,293,294] , expect for the JG/T 472–2015 model  [287]  and the Savinoa et al. model  [291] . However, the latter two models do not predict the strength of SFRC with hybrid types of steel fibers. Therefore, a general model for the tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC is still required to fully understand the physical mechanisms by which fibers enhance the mechanical properties of SFRC.

The fiber bridging stress model is a well-known framework used to evaluate the fiber bridging effect by calculating the bridging stress transferred across a crack with a given crack opening displacement  [295] . This framework connects micro-scale material parameters to macro-scale mechanical performance. The model is typically derived by combining the bond-slip model of a single fiber embedded in a concrete matrix with a specific fiber distribution  [295–298] .

The bond properties of the fiber-matrix interface are usually studied experimentally using single fiber pullout tests  [52,299–342] . As the pullout behavior of steel fibers is influenced by various factors such as embedded length, radius, geometry, orientation, material properties, and interfacial characteristics, the experimental results exhibit significant variability. Based on these results, some scholars have proposed bond-slip models to predict the pullout behavior of single steel fibers  [294,299,300,343–347] . However, these models are often based on limited experimental data and typically focus on specific types of fibers or concrete matrices. Thus, the universality of these models still requires comprehensive verification on large validation datasets.

In this paper, a smeared fiber-matrix pullout strength model is developed within the fiber bridging stress framework, based on a comprehensive database of 965 pullout test results for single steel fibers embedded in a cementitious matrix. From this model, formulas for predicting the tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC are derived. The effectiveness and accuracy of these formulas are verified using two complementary databases of tested tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC, containing 321 and 1595 results, respectively.

sections.heading: Bridging force of single straight, hooked-end or twisted steel fiber with various embedded angles
Database of pull-out test of single steel fiber embedded in cementitious matrix
paragraphs: A single steel fiber’s bridging force is usually measured using the pull-out test. To model the maximum bridging force of steel fiber, a large database was built, which contains the information regarding the compressive strength of the matrix, fiber characteristics (e.g., type, diameter, length, tensile strength, elastic modulus), embedment length and inclination angle of fibers, failure type, average bond strength. A total of 965 data points were compiled in the database, which were collected from 45 individual sources  [52,299–342] .

As shown in  
                            Table 1 , the pull-out tests of various types of steel fibers embedded in the cement matrix are reported in these references. The straight, hooked (including both hooked and half-hooked) and twisted fibers rank in the top three, accounting for 46.11 %, 30.98 %, and 15.13 %, respectively. The total proportion of these three types of fibers reaches 92.23 %. Therefore, this study focuses on the bridging force of these three types of steel fibers. Moreover, the database covers a relatively wide range of compressive strengths of cement matrix  f 
                            c , ranging from 16.7 to 262 MPa.

sections.heading: Compressive strength formula for SFRC
paragraphs:
Plain concrete under a longitudinal compression is in a uniaxial state of stress. The longitudinal strains from this load induce transverse tensile strains, potentially causing vertical cracking. As the material approaches its uniaxial compressive capacity, both the transverse strains and vertical cracks reach their limit  [355] . Transverse reinforcement can provide external confinement pressure to limit the lateral expansion of concrete, thereby improving its compressive strength and toughness. A similar enhancement is observed in SFRC, where the bridging force provided by the steel fibers internally confines the lateral expansion of concrete and the propagation of longitudinal cracks. Tested tensile strength database of SFRC
paragraphs:
To verify the proposed model, the tested tensile strength of SFRC reported from 41 individual sources was collected into a large database containing 333 test results  [12–51] . As shown in

Specimens with single-type fibers make up 90.9 % of the total, with proportions of straight fibers, hooked-end fibers, and twisted fibers at 29.28 %, 40.19 %, and 21.50 %, respectively. The minimum and maximum fiber volume fractions are 0.5 % and 6 %, respectively. Additionally, the strength of the plain concrete ranges from 21.44 MPa to 220 MPa.

sections.heading: Comparison results and discussion
paragraphs:
Using the proposed model and the existing models mentioned above, the tensile strength predictions for the samples in the database were calculated.  
                         Fig. 10  presents the comparison between the tested and calculated results. The mean value and coefficient of variance (CoV) of the ratio between the calculated and tested results along with the average absolute error (AAE) are also shown in the figure.

Generally, almost all models, except for the JG/T 472–2015 model, provide a relatively conservative prediction of the tensile strength of SFRC. The mean value of the calculation-to-experiment ratio of the proposed model was 0.91, which was the closest to the experimental results. It also has the lowest value of AAE ( − 1.17 MPa). The JG/T 472–2015 model overestimates the tensile strength of SFRC, with a mean calculation-to-experiment ratio of 1.39. The value of AAE is 2.25 MPa. Meanwhile, as shown in  Fig. 10 , the results calculated by all models exhibit significant variability. The proposed model, JG/T 472–2015 model, and Padmarajaiah model had the lowest CoV of the calculation-to-experiment ratio, with a value of 0.39. The prediction of the Savino et al. model had the highest CoV of the calculation-to-experiment ratio, with a value of 0.56.

To demonstrate the performance of the proposed model across different fiber types,  
                         Fig. 11  provides a comparison between the experimental and calculated results using solely straight, hooked-end, and twisted fibers, as well as the hybrids. It can be observed from  Fig. 11  that the proposed model performed well for straight and hooked-end fibers. The mean values of the calculation-to-experiment ratio are 0.95 and 1.03, respectively, with CoVs of 0.30 and 0.37, and with AAEs of −0.98 MPa and −0.44 MPa, respectively. However, the model significantly underestimates the tensile strength of SFRC with twisted or hybrid fibers. The mean calculation-to-experiment ratios are 0.59 for twisted fibers and 0.63 for hybrid fibers, with AAEs of −2.88 MPa and −4.19 MPa. Note that, the predictions for twisted fibers exhibited considerable variability, with a CoV of 0.50 for the calculation-to-experiment ratio.

As shown in  Table 1 , there are a total of 146 tests involving twisted fibers in the pullout experiment database, accounting for approximately 15 % of the total. This is one-third and one-half of the number of experiments involving straight fibers and hooked-end fibers, respectively. As the result, the bond strength model for twisted fiber exhibited the greatest variability, with a CoV of 0.45, as shown in  Fig. 6 . Further, more pullout experiments on twisted fibers in concrete are recommended to be conducted to improve the prediction accuracy.

sections.heading: Comparison results and discussion
paragraphs:
The comparison between the tested compressive strength in the database and their predictions calculated by using the proposed model and existing models mentioned above is plotted in  
                         Fig. 12 . The mean value and CoV of the calculation-to-experiment ratio with AEEs are also shown in this figure.

As shown in  Fig. 12 , all the models perform well. The mean values and CoV of the calculation-to-experiment ratio ranged from 0.93 to 1.00 and 0.12–0.17, respectively. The model by Abbass et al. provided the closest predictions to the experimental results, with a mean calculation-to-experiment ratio of 1.00. The proposed model had the lowest CoV at 0.12, corresponding to a mean value of 0.93.

To study the effect of fiber volume fraction on the performance of the proposed model,  
                         Fig. 13  plots the relationship between fiber volume fraction and the calculation-to-experiment ratio of the compressive strength of SFRC. It can be seen that the proposed model performs well when the fiber volume fraction is no more than 2 %. However, when  V 
                         f  is between 2 % and 3 %, the predictions become more dispersed, with the CoV increasing up to 0.27. Moreover, when  V 
                         f  exceeds 3 %, the proposed model tends to overestimate the compressive strength, with a mean calculation-to-experiment ratio of 1.22. The proposed model assumes a homogeneous distribution of steel fibers within the concrete matrix. However, as fiber volume increases beyond a certain level (3 %–5 %), achieving homogeneous distribution becomes challenging during the concrete mixing process  [291,297] . Therefore, fibers are not always beneficial to the compressive strength of SFRC.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study presents a smeared fiber-matrix pullout strength model allowing to predict the mechanical properties of SFRC with various types of steel fibers. The model, developed within the fiber bridging stress framework, is based on a pull-out test database of single steel fibers embedded in a cementitious matrix, encompassing a total of 965 test results. Using this model, tensile and compressive strength formulas for SFRC are derived. To evaluate the formulas’ effectiveness and accuracy, separate databases of tested tensile and compressive strengths were established, containing 321 and 1595 test results, respectively. The derived formulas are used to predict the strength of samples in these databases and are compared with existing models.
Based on the content presented in this work, the following conclusions can be drawn:

1. 
                            The proposed model well describes the smeared fiber-matrix pullout strength of SFRC, accommodating both single and hybrid types of steel fibers. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The derived formulas effectively predict the tensile and compressive strengths of SFRC. The mean calculation-to-experiment ratios for tensile and compressive strengths are 0.91 and 0.93, respectively, with corresponding CoVs of 0.39 and 0.12. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The proposed model is supported by the pullout test database. Therefore, its accuracy and reliability depends on the amount and the quality of the tested data. In further, more pullout experiments on twisted fiber will be conducted or collected to improve the prediction accuracy. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The proposed compressive strength formula is suitable for predicting the compressive strength of SFRC with a fiber volume fraction is no more than 3 %. When fiber volume increases beyond a certain level, achieving homogeneous distribution becomes challenging during the concrete mixing process. The homogeneous distribution assumption adopted in this model tends to overestimate the compressive strength of SFRC.
